source.title: Automatically Interpreting Millions of Features in Large Language Models
source.authors: Gonçalo Paulo; Alex Troy Mallen; C. Juang; Nora Belrose

record.tranche_reason: Applies automated interpretation and scoring to SAE features in Gemma 2 9b and Llama 3.1 8b, extending discussion of sparse dictionary features to LLMs. It does not reproduce the toy-model superposition method.
record.gate_note: The paper measures how well natural-language interpretations identify SAE features and compares the scores with neuron interpretations. This bears on the SAE-feature branch of V4, but is not a direct test of whether SAEs recover the model's complete or canonical units. The discussion of polysemanticity and feature splitting cites prior work; cited results are not rows. The intervention-score plots concern interpretation of intervention effects, not superposition geometry.
record.test_reason: Table A10 compares automated-interpretation scores of SAE features with neurons in Gemma 2 9b and Llama 3.1 8b, against random-interpretation and random-SAE baselines. That is indirect evidence on V4's SAE branch. Most of the paper evaluates scoring methods, so only this comparison and the layer and intervention results bear on the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors present scalable scoring methods (fuzzing, detection, embedding, surprisal, intervention) with distinct limitations, and give prompt-design guidelines. Intervention scoring reveals output features that context-based methods miss. Incidentally, SAE features (more so in larger SAEs) are significantly more interpretable than neurons, even top-k-sparsified ones.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE training on LLM activations followed by automated natural-language interpretation and scoring; it does not use the original toy-network setup or test overlapping directions.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretation scores vary with SAE size and location, model layer, scorer or explainer choice, and activation-example sampling strategy. Table A10 also reports different scores for Gemma 2 9b and Llama 3.1 8b.

fits_no_version.finding: On RPJv2 at 256-token contexts, 15% of the 131k Gemma SAE's features never activate and 30% activate fewer than 200 times. On the Pile only 1% never activate. The 16k SAE has about 10% rare features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which SAE features appear depends on the data distribution; larger SAEs learn more dataset-specific features.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The evidence for V4 is indirect: interpretation scores are proxies and do not establish complete or canonical recovery of model features. The reported scores are medians with interquartile ranges; Table A10 does not state the sample count for each comparison.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported score comparisons and intervention-scoring results (Tables A3–A9, Figures 2–3 and A6–A7) primarily evaluate interpretation-generation or scorer methods rather than whether dictionaries recover model features. Figure-only intervention results are also not measurements of V4's recovery claim.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, geometry or sparsity transition.
All: capacity competition is not examined.
All: the causes of polysemanticity are not examined.
How features are distributed across neurons is not measured directly. SAE reconstruction quality and feature recovery against ground truth are not assessed.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not tested. The dead and rare feature counts are only descriptive.
All: whether features are one-dimensional is not examined.

missing.what: Interpretation scores by layer (earlier layers lower, then flat)
Intervention scores of trained SAE features exceed those of a random TopK SAE and of shuffled interpretations, especially at higher KL
Residual-stream SAEs score slightly higher than MLP SAEs

record.verdict_notes: The SAE-vs-neuron comparison is a side result in a methods paper; the evidence is interpretability as judged by an LLM scorer, not ground-truth recovery. The reader's limits_scope label is replaced: its reason described unmeasured aspects, which belong under untested. A real scope limit (early layers) comes from the text instead. The Llama SAE feature count is inconsistent (65k in Appendix E vs 262k in Table A10). Sample counts for Table A10 are not stated; Fig A5 suggests about 300 features per layer.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure, and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.

The paper tests interpretation scores for SAE features as indirect evidence of dictionary-readable features. It does not measure how features are distributed across neurons or establish feature recovery as complete or canonical.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.
